exercises.prompt: The bakery cooperative sends four questions. Which one is a **causal** question?

options.label: How many loaves did Market sell on Saturdays in April?
options.feedback: Not yet. This asks what happened: a descriptive question, answered by careful counting.

options.label: How many loaves will Station sell next Saturday?
options.feedback: Not yet. This asks what will happen if the world goes on as before: a predictive question.

options.label: Did opening an hour earlier at Hilltop increase its sales?
options.feedback: Yes. It asks what difference a change made, comparing what happened with what would have happened otherwise. That needs a comparison that rules out other explanations, ideally an experiment.

options.label: How many loaves should Riverside bake on Sundays?
options.feedback: Not yet. This asks what to do: a prescriptive question. It combines a prediction of demand with the costs of baking too many or too few.

hints: Causal questions are about the effect of a change: 'what would happen if we did X instead of Y?'
Only one option mentions something the bakery changed.
exercises.solution:
**C** is causal: it asks about the effect of a change (opening earlier). Before-and-after sales at one shop cannot answer it on their own, because the weather, the season or a new office nearby may have changed at the same time; a fair answer needs a comparison group or an experiment.

A is **descriptive** (what happened), B is **predictive** (what will happen if nothing changes) and D is **prescriptive** (what should we do), which combines a prediction with costs and values, as in the newsvendor calculation of the lesson.

exercises.prompt:
On ten recent Saturdays when it did **not** sell out, a shop's demand was

88, 132, 97, 120, 141, 105, 126, 113, 150, 101 loaves.

A loaf costs 0.30 to bake and sells for 1.00; unsold loaves earn nothing. Treating these ten days as equally likely, what is the **smallest** number of loaves that maximises the average profit?

feedback.message: Not yet. 120 is the 60th percentile, which is right when a loaf costs 0.40. Here it costs 0.30, so the critical ratio is (1.00 − 0.30) / 1.00 = 0.7.

Close: 132 earns exactly the same average profit as 126, because in between, each extra loaf sells with probability 0.3 and earns 0.30 on average, the same as it costs. The question asks for the smallest best value.
Not yet. That is the mean demand. The best quantity is a percentile of demand, not its average.

hints: An extra loaf is worth baking while the chance it sells, P(demand > q), is more than cost / price = 0.3.
Sort the demands: 88, 97, 101, 105, 113, 120, 126, 132, 141, 150. For which q do at most 3 of the 10 days have demand above q?
exercises.solution:
An extra loaf earns $1.00 \times P(D > q)$ on average and costs $0.30$, so keep adding loaves while $P(D > q) > 0.3$, that is, while more than 3 of the 10 days had demand above $q$. Equivalently, bake the $(1.00 - 0.30)/1.00 = 70$th percentile.

Sorted: 88, 97, 101, 105, 113, 120, **126**, 132, 141, 150. At $q = 125$, four days (126, 132, 141, 150) exceed $q$, so one more loaf is still worth baking. At $q = 126$, only three days exceed it: the next loaf sells with probability 0.3, earning 0.30 on average and costing 0.30, so it neither helps nor hurts. Average profit is flat from 126 to 132 (both give 75.0 per day on average over these ten days) and falls after that. The smallest best quantity is **126**, the 7th smallest value.

exercises.prompt: On days when a shop sells out, the sales figure tells you only that demand was *at least* the number baked. What do statisticians call data like this? (One word is enough.)
hints: The same word is used for survival times when a study ends before the event happens.
The true value has been cut off, or hidden, above a limit.
exercises.solution: **Censored** (more precisely, *right-censored*): we observe $\min(D, 120)$ instead of the demand $D$, so on sold-out days we know only that $D \ge 120$. Survival analysis has methods built for exactly this situation (a patient still alive when a study ends is censored in the same way); see [survival analysis](/en/statistics/survival-analysis/) in Lumenary Statistics. Treating censored values as if they were the real values biases estimates downwards.

exercises.prompt: In the lesson's test weeks, the plan built on raw sales wasted the fewest loaves (397, against 497 for the plan built on estimated demand). Why is it still the worse plan?

options.label: It learned from censored sales, so it bakes too little on busy days: it sold out on 54 of 112 shop-days, turned away 708 customers and made less profit.
options.feedback: Yes. Low waste is easy to achieve by baking too little; the question was about profit (and, implicitly, customers), and on both counts it does worse.

options.label: 397 is not really smaller than 497, because the difference is within the noise.
options.feedback: Not yet. The difference may well be noisy, but that is not why the plan is worse: even with less waste, it loses more in turned-away customers than it saves in bread.

options.label: The sales-based plan uses the wrong percentile.
options.feedback: Not yet. Both plans use the 60th percentile. They differ in what they take the percentile *of*: recorded sales or estimated demand.

options.label: Wasted loaves do not cost anything, because they go to a food bank.
options.feedback: Not yet. Giving them away is good, but each still cost 0.40 to make; that cost is in the profit calculation.

hints: What was the cooperative's real objective: least waste, or something else?
Look at the other columns of the table: sell-out days, unmet demand and profit.
exercises.solution: **A.** Minimising waste alone has a trivial answer (bake nothing). The sales-based plan learned from data censored at 120, so on the busiest days it believed demand was 120 and baked too little: 54 sell-out days and 708 customers turned away, against 43 and 256 for the plan built on estimated demand. Each lost sale costs 0.60 of margin, more than the 0.40 an unsold loaf costs, so its lower waste does not make up for it, and its profit is lower (6,093 against 6,324). A headline such as "waste down 86%" would have been true and badly misleading.

exercises.prompt: Which of these make an analysis more **reproducible**? Select all that apply.

options.label: Pinning exact package versions in a lock file
options.feedback: Yes. Packages change behaviour between versions; a lock file lets anyone recreate your environment.

options.label: Seeding every random generator and recording the seed
options.feedback: Yes. Simulations, train/test splits and model initialisation all use random numbers; a recorded seed makes them repeatable.

options.label: Saving a hash (fingerprint) of the input data with the results
options.feedback: Yes. It proves which data produced which result, and reveals silent edits.

options.label: Fixing typos directly in the raw CSV file so the code stays simple
options.feedback: Not yet. Hand edits leave no record; nobody can tell what changed or redo it on next month's export. Keep raw data read-only and make every fix in code.

options.label: Restarting the notebook kernel and running all cells from the top before sharing
options.feedback: Yes. It removes hidden state left by cells run out of order or deleted.

options.label: Sending the final chart as an image and deleting the code that made it
options.feedback: Not yet. Without the code nobody, including you, can check or regenerate the chart.

hints: Ask of each practice: could someone else rerun the analysis from the raw data and get the same numbers?
Two of the six options destroy information that a rerun would need.
exercises.solution:
**A, B, C and E.** Each removes a reason a rerun could give different numbers: different package versions (A), different random numbers (B), different input data (C), and hidden notebook state (E).

**D** and **F** make things worse: a hand edit to raw data cannot be audited or repeated on the next export, and deleting code makes the result impossible to check. Raw data should be read-only, with every correction written as code and committed to version control.

exercises.reference:
import pandas as pd

def clean_sales(raw):
    """Return a cleaned copy of a till export with columns date, shop, baked, sold."""
    df = raw.copy()
    df["shop"] = df["shop"].str.strip().str.title()
    df = df.drop_duplicates()
    df = df[df["sold"].between(0, df["baked"])].copy()
    df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%d/%m/%Y")
    df["sold_out"] = df["sold"] == df["baked"]
    return df.reset_index(drop=True)
hints: Start with `df = raw.copy()`; then `df["shop"].str.strip().str.title()` fixes the names.
`df.drop_duplicates()` removes exact duplicates; `df["sold"].between(0, df["baked"])` is a Boolean mask of plausible rows (both ends included).
`pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%d/%m/%Y")` parses day-first dates unambiguously. Finish with `df.reset_index(drop=True)`.
exercises.solution:
Apply the steps in order, on a copy, and keep each one a single readable line:

```python
import pandas as pd

def clean_sales(raw):
    df = raw.copy()
    df["shop"] = df["shop"].str.strip().str.title()
    df = df.drop_duplicates()
    df = df[df["sold"].between(0, df["baked"])].copy()
    df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%d/%m/%Y")
    df["sold_out"] = df["sold"] == df["baked"]
    return df.reset_index(drop=True)
```

The order matters: `"hilltop "` and `"Hilltop"` are different strings until step 1, so deduplicating first would keep both copies of that day. Giving the date format explicitly matters too: without it, `12/03/2026` could be read as 3 December. The `.copy()` after filtering makes it explicit that we are working on a new table before adding a column. In a real project each step would also log how many rows it changed, as the lesson's code does, so the cleaning can be reported and checked.

exercises.prompt:
Write `best_bake(demands, price, cost)`. `demands` is a list of past daily demands (positive integers), each treated as equally likely tomorrow. Baking `q` loaves on a day with demand `d` earns `price * min(d, q) - cost * q`. Return the **integer** `q` between 0 and `max(demands)` that maximises the **average** profit over the past demands; if several values tie, return the **smallest**.

Compute it by trying every `q` (do not just use a percentile formula), then check that your answers agree with the critical-ratio rule from the lesson.
exercises.tests:
past = [80, 95, 100, 102, 110, 120, 125, 130, 140, 150]
assert best_bake(past, 1.00, 0.40) == 120, best_bake(past, 1.00, 0.40)
assert best_bake(past, 1.00, 0.10) == 140, "cheap loaves: bake more"
assert best_bake(past, 1.00, 0.90) == 80, "expensive loaves: bake less"
assert best_bake([88, 132, 97, 120, 141, 105, 126, 113, 150, 101], 1.00, 0.30) == 126
assert best_bake([50], 2.0, 1.0) == 50
assert best_bake([10, 20], 1.0, 0.5) == 10, "when several quantities tie, return the smallest"
assert isinstance(best_bake(past, 1.0, 0.4), int)
hints: Write a helper `avg_profit(q)` that averages `price * min(d, q) - cost * q` over the demands.
Loop `q` over `range(0, max(demands) + 1)` and keep the best so far. Only replace it when a new `q` is *strictly* better, so ties keep the smaller value.
Profits are floats, so two equal profits may differ in the last digit (0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3). Compare with a small tolerance, such as `p > best + 1e-9`.
